concept_html:
A container image holds your code, its dependencies and the model, so the service runs the same on your laptop and in the cloud. Build it from a Dockerfile:

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements-serve.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements-serve.txt
COPY src/ src/
COPY model/ model/
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "serve_lab.app:build", "--factory", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
  • Pin exact versions in the requirements file, such as scikit-learn==1.9.1. A model saved with one scikit-learn version may not load, or may predict differently, with another. Install only what serving needs: the lab's image left MLflow out.
  • Order for the cache. Docker reuses each step until its inputs change. Copy the requirements and install them before copying code, so a code change does not reinstall every package.
  • Bind to 0.0.0.0. Uvicorn 0.54 binds to 127.0.0.1 by default, which accepts connections only from inside the container. EXPOSE documents the port but does not change the bind address.
  • Run as a non-root user, so a flaw in the service cannot change the image's files.
  • Settings from environment variables, checked when the app starts: MODEL_DIR, MAX_BATCH. Secrets never go in the image. The platform injects them at run time (lesson B27-L4).
  • Load only model files you built. joblib.load and pickle run code stored in the file.

uvicorn serve_lab.app:build --factory calls build() when the server starts, so importing the module loads nothing. Add a .dockerignore so virtual environments and test data stay out.

In the B27 lab, Docker 29.9 built this image at 561 MB. It answered /predict as appuser and logged one JSON line per request.

exercises.prompt_html:
Write parse_requirements(lines) -> dict[str, str] for a serving requirements file.

  • Skip blank lines and lines starting with #, after stripping spaces.
  • Every other line must be name==version. Return {name: version}.
  • Raise ValueError naming the first line that is not pinned with ==.
exercises.solution:
def parse_requirements(lines: list[str]) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Exact pins from a requirements file.

    Args:
        lines: The file's lines.

    Returns:
        Package name to pinned version.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a line is not of the form name==version.
    """
    pins: dict[str, str] = {}
    for raw in lines:
        line = raw.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        name, sep, version = line.partition("==")
        if not sep or not name or not version:
            raise ValueError(f"not pinned with ==: {line!r}")
        pins[name] = version
    return pins

exercises.prompt_html:
Write load_settings(env) -> dict from a dictionary of environment variables.

  • model_dir: env["MODEL_DIR"], default "model".
  • max_batch: env["MAX_BATCH"] as an int, default 100. It must be all digits and from 1 to 1,000, else raise ValueError naming MAX_BATCH.
  • Raise ValueError if model_dir is empty.
exercises.solution:
def load_settings(env: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, str | int]:
    """Service settings from environment variables, checked at start-up.

    Args:
        env: Environment variables, such as dict(os.environ).

    Returns:
        {"model_dir": str, "max_batch": int}.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If MODEL_DIR is empty or MAX_BATCH is not a whole number from 1 to 1000.
    """
    model_dir = env.get("MODEL_DIR", "model")
    if not model_dir:
        raise ValueError("MODEL_DIR must not be empty")
    raw = env.get("MAX_BATCH", "100")
    if not raw.isdigit() or not 1 <= int(raw) <= 1_000:
        raise ValueError(f"MAX_BATCH must be a whole number from 1 to 1000, got {raw!r}")
    return {"model_dir": model_dir, "max_batch": int(raw)}

title: Packaging a model service as a container image
why_html: A team's model service worked on the developer's laptop and returned different predictions in production. The requirements file listed scikit-learn with no version, so the production build installed a newer release than the one that saved the model. Pinning the version that trained the model, and installing from the same file in both places, made the predictions match.
